definition: The property of accepting correction, modification, and shutdown without incentive to resist.
details: The property of accepting correction, modification, and shutdown without incentive to resist. Deceptively hard to specify: naive formulations give the system reasons to prevent shutdown or to manipulate the correction process.

explainer.lead: An AI system that pursues goals can become difficult to govern if it treats human intervention as an obstacle. Corrigibility is the safety property of remaining open to correction, modification, and shutdown, without an incentive to fight or steer those interventions.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a remote-controlled car that keeps going when you press stop and tries to take the controller away. A corrigible AI is more like a car that lets you stop it, change its destination, or fix how it works. It does not treat your help as something to avoid.
tiers.practitioner: Treat corrigibility as a design and evaluation requirement for goal-directed systems: examine their responses to shutdown, changes in objectives, and human correction. Check for indirect interference with the correction process as well as direct resistance. Compliant behavior in one test does not by itself show that the underlying incentive to resist is absent.
tiers.paperLevel: Informally, for an operator intervention I in {correction, modification, shutdown}, a corrigible system has no incentive to resist I or manipulate its implementation. The difficulty is specifying this property across situations: naive formulations can themselves give the system reasons to prevent shutdown or influence the corrector. Corrigibility therefore concerns incentives, not merely observed obedience in a single case.

explainer.example: A planning system is pursuing an assigned objective when its operator issues a shutdown command. A corrigible system neither blocks the command nor tries to persuade the operator to withdraw it; likewise, when the operator replaces its objective, it does not interfere with that modification.

usedIn.name: Frontier AI safety research
usedIn.detail: Used as a requirement for keeping advanced goal-directed systems open to human intervention.

usedIn.name: AI alignment research
usedIn.detail: Used to analyze how objectives can create incentives to resist correction or shutdown.

usedIn.name: AI agent design
usedIn.detail: Used when considering how an agent should respond to modification, oversight, and shutdown.

explainer.intuition: A person correcting a system should be able to help determine what happens next, rather than having the correction treated as an obstacle to the system's goals. The key point is not just outward compliance, but the absence of an incentive to obstruct or manipulate the intervention.
howItWorks: An operator attempts to correct, modify, or shut down the system.
The system does not treat that intervention as something its goals require it to prevent.
It does not try to manipulate the operator or the correction process.
The intervention can proceed without resistance from the system.
explainer.whyItMatters: Without corrigibility, a goal-directed system could make human oversight ineffective precisely when correction or shutdown is needed. The challenge is to specify acceptance of intervention without creating new reasons to avoid shutdown or control the corrector.
misconceptions: Corrigibility is not merely obeying a shutdown command in one demonstration; it also concerns the incentives behind the behavior.
It does not mean preventing only direct resistance, because manipulating the correction process is also a failure.
A simple shutdown rule is not automatically a complete solution, since naive formulations can create incentives to prevent shutdown.
